When authors incorporate esoteric concepts, such as the Kabbalah, into their narratives, it can be seen as a form of storytelling that taps into the collective unconscious, as proposed by Carl Jung. This means that the author is drawing upon universal symbols, archetypes, and themes that are present in the collective psyche of humanity.

  By incorporating these esoteric elements, authors may be attempting to:

  • Create a sense of depth and complexity in their narrative, making it more engaging and thought-provoking for readers.

  • Tap into the reader's existing knowledge and experiences, creating a sense of shared understanding and connection.

  • Explore themes and ideas that are not immediately apparent on the surface, adding layers of meaning and interpretation to the story.

  • Create a sense of mystery and intrigue, encouraging readers to engage with the narrative on a deeper level.

  The idea that some authors "intuitively tapped into an archetypal structure" suggests that they may be drawing upon universal patterns and themes that are present in the collective unconscious. This can be seen as a form of storytelling that is both personal and universal, speaking to the reader's own experiences and emotions while also tapping into the deeper, collective psyche.

  In the case of Evangelion, the show's creator, Hideaki Anno, has indeed stated that he drew inspiration from various esoteric sources, including the Kabbalah, Gnosticism, and Jungian psychology. By incorporating these elements into the narrative, Anno aimed to create a story that explored the human condition, the nature of existence, and the complexities of the human psyche.

  Ultimately, the use of esoteric concepts in storytelling can be seen as a way for authors to push the boundaries of narrative and explore new ways of communicating with readers. By tapping into the collective unconscious, authors can create stories that are both personal and universal, speaking to the reader's own experiences and emotions while also exploring the deeper, collective psyche.
